intro: The reverse of Isabelle Nef’s Oiseau-Lyre disc has the second gigue, headed 2e Gigue, of the D minor suite in Élisabeth Jacquet de La Guerre’s Pièces de clavecin of 1707. It is in six-eight time. The first strain, of 25 bars, is played twice, and the second, of 38 bars, once. The Allemande on the other side comes from the G major suite of the same book.

sections.label: A · First strain, repeated
sections.mNote: The first strain, played a second time.

cues.title: 2e Gigue, first strain
cues.text: The 2e Gigue is in six-eight time and in two strains, each with a repeat sign. The first strain has 25 bars. It begins on an upbeat A, reaches an E major chord with G♯ in bars 23–24 and closes on an A major chord.
cues.evidence: Identified by comparison with the printed score; the labels, the Internet Archive record and the discographies name only a Gigue. Source: Jacquet de La Guerre, Pièces de clavecin qui peuvent se joüer sur le viollon (Paris, 1707), Suite in D minor, 2e Gigue. First edition, printed pages 13–14 (scan of the Bibliothèque nationale de France copy, IMSLP 111449: http://conquest.imslp.info/files/imglnks/usimg/5/55/IMSLP111449-PMLP62189-Jacquet_de_La_Guerre_-_Pieces_de_Clavecin_qui_peuvent_se_jouer_sur_le_Viollon,_1707.pdf). Steve Wiberg’s edition, Due West Editions, 2009, printed pages 16–17, whose bar numbers are used here (IMSLP 28300: http://conquest.imslp.info/files/imglnks/usimg/4/40/IMSLP28300-PMLP62189-LaGuerre_PiecesDeClavecin_1707_Complete.pdf). In the recording the pitch is about 25 cents above A = 440, so the key sounds as written. The upbeat A5 is at about 2.6 s. Bar 1 begins at about 3.0 s (right hand F5, D5, A4, F5; left hand D3, F3, A3, D4) and bar 2, over an E in the bass with C♯5, B♭4 and G4 above it, at about 4.7 s. Bar 6 begins at about 11.2 s, after the B♭5 that ends bar 5, so a bar lasts about 1.6 s, or about 75 dotted crotchets a minute. In bar 23 the right hand falls G♯–F♯–E over an E chord from about 37.7 s, and the A major chord of bar 25 (first ending) sounds from about 41 s.

cues.title: First strain repeated
cues.text: The first strain is played again from its upbeat A, at about 0:43, and closes on the same A major chord. The second ending, bar 26, leads into the second strain.
cues.evidence: Wiberg’s edition, printed page 16 (first edition, printed page 13): bar 25 is the first ending, which closes on a chord of A, C♯ and E and an upbeat A5 into the repeat, and bar 26 is the second ending. In the recording the upbeat A5 of the repeat sounds at about 42.7 s, the A major chord of bar 25 at about 81.3 s, and the second strain begins at about 83.7 s. The first strain takes about 40 s on each pass.

cues.title: Second strain, bars 27–64
cues.text: The second strain, headed Reprise, has 38 bars against 25 in the first. The right hand begins F5–E5–D5–E5. The recording plays the strain once and omits its printed repeat; it ends on a D minor chord.
cues.evidence: Wiberg’s edition, printed pages 16–17 (first edition, printed pages 13–14): the Reprise runs from bar 27 to bar 64, the first ending, which closes with a repeat sign; the second ending is bar 65. In the recording bar 27 begins at about 83.7 s with a grace note leading to F5, held for a crotchet, then E5, D5 and E5. The strain takes about 60 s, 1.6 s a bar as in the first strain, and no second pass follows.

cues.title: Final chord
cues.text: The gigue ends on a D minor chord at about 2:23, held for about four seconds. Surface noise fills the rest of the file.
cues.evidence: Wiberg’s edition, the end of the second strain (bars 64–65): a chord of D, F and A over a D bass. In the recording the chord (D3, A3, F5) sounds from about 142.9 s and is held to about 147 s. After it the recording carries only surface noise, with a loud thump at about 152 s.

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: The Bibliothèque nationale de France record reads “Isabelle Nef, clav.” and gives her dates as 1898–1976. The make of the instrument is not established.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: 2e Gigue of the Suite in D minor in Jacquet de La Guerre’s Pièces de clavecin qui peuvent se joüer sur le viollon (Paris, 1707), EJG.05, played with the first strain twice and the second strain once, without its repeat
fields.note: The labels, the Internet Archive record, the BnF catalogue and the Oiseau-Lyre discography on medieval.org name only a Gigue and an Allemande; none names a book, suite or key, so the identification rests on comparing the recording with the printed scores. Pitch tracking of the transfer (mains hum removed; tuning 25 cents above A = 440, interquartile range 20–30 cents, as on the reverse side) finds an upbeat A5 at about 2.6 s; bar 1 from about 3.0 s with F5 in the right hand over left-hand D3, F3, A3 and D4; bar 2 over an E in the bass with C♯5, B♭4 and G4 above it; an E major harmony with G♯ at about 37.7–40 s, followed by an A major chord (A, C♯, E) at about 41–42.5 s; the same strain again from an upbeat A5 at about 42.7 s; a second strain from about 83.7 s that ends on a D minor chord at about 143 s; and no second pass of that strain. The first strain takes about 40 s and the second about 60 s. This agrees with the 2e Gigue of the D minor suite in the 1707 book (first edition, printed pages 13–14; Wiberg’s edition, printed pages 16–17): six-eight time, a right-hand upbeat A5, bar 1 on F5 over left-hand D, F, A and D, a first strain of 25 bars that reaches an E major chord with G♯ in bars 23–24 and closes on A major, and a second strain of 38 bars (27–64) that closes on D minor; at about 1.6 s a bar, 25 and 38 bars take about 40 s and 60 s. The earlier reading of the Gigue as centred on A minor, with a first strain ending on E with G♯, took the E major harmony before the A major chord of bar 25 for the close of the strain. Of the nine gigues and doubles in the two books, this is the only one in six-eight; the others are in 6/4 (1687: D minor, A minor, F major; 1707: D minor, its Double, G major), in 3/4 (1687, first G minor gigue) or in common time (1687, second G minor gigue). The file sounds a quarter of a semitone sharp, so there is no whole-tone offset that would turn a G minor or F major gigue into the recording. The earlier proposals, the F major gigue of 1687 (EJG.04) and the A minor gigue (EJG.03), could not be reproduced. The Allemande on the reverse comes from the other suite of the 1707 book, in G major, so the two sides of the disc are from different suites; no source states the pairing.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The recording date is not stated in the sources consulted. The BnF record dates the disc 1942; an Oiseau-Lyre discography after Jim Davidson’s Lyrebird Rising (1994) gives its release as 1938 or 1939, recording site and date unknown (https://medieval.org/emfaq/cds/lol75.htm). The Internet Archive upload date of 25 October 2018 is not a session date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Digitised at 78 rpm with four stylus sizes, flat and equalised; the engineer’s preferred version is the one offered, as a variable-bitrate MP3 derived from a 24-bit FLAC.
fields.note: The pitch of the file is about 25 cents above A = 440 (interquartile range 20–30 cents), as on the other side of the disc, and the identified score is in D minor, which sounds as written. The offset cannot be divided between the harpsichord’s tuning and the speed of the disc or its transfer; no speed correction was applied here.

fields.value: Out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Jacquet de La Guerre died in 1729. This is a term calculation, not clearance of every edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial EU public-domain basis for a disc dated 1942 by the Bibliothèque nationale de France (release in 1938 or 1939 according to an Oiseau-Lyre discography), under the programme’s pre-1963 recording rule.
fields.note: The BnF date is a catalogue date for the disc, not an independently verified first-publication date; an Oiseau-Lyre discography (https://medieval.org/emfaq/cds/lol75.htm, after Davidson’s Lyrebird Rising) places the release in 1938 or 1939, and the label began issuing discs in December 1937. Either date is before 1963. The Gallica record marks its own digital copy as public domain; the Internet Archive item carries no licence. US first-publication evidence and US status are not established.

composer.epithet: Parisian harpsichordist and composer who played for Louis XIV as a child and published harpsichord suites, violin sonatas, cantatas and the opera Céphale et Procris.
facts: In Paris with her father, the organist Claude Jacquet; harpsichord and singing at court from the age of five
Played for Louis XIV as a child; three or four years at Madame de Montespan’s side; left the court on her marriage in 1684
Taught and gave concerts in her apartment on the Île Saint-Louis; married to the organist Marin de La Guerre
Harpsichord suites, trio and violin sonatas, cantatas, the opera Céphale et Procris and a lost Te Deum

quote.text: Finding in me at the age of five some disposition for the harpsichord, you ordered that care be taken to bring me up in it.
quote.source: Élisabeth Jacquet to Louis XIV, dedication of Les Pièces de clavessin, Paris, 1687; our translation

composer.background:
Élisabeth Jacquet was baptised in Paris on 17 March 1665. Her father, Claude Jacquet, was organist of Saint-Louis-en-l’Île, on the island in the Seine now called the Île Saint-Louis, and Catherine Cessac describes him as an excellent teacher. All four of his children became musicians: Pierre and Nicolas as organists, Anne as an instrumentalist in the household of Mademoiselle de Guise, and Élisabeth as a harpsichordist and singer. A great-uncle, Jehan Jacquet, and an uncle, also named Claude, were makers of musical instruments.

The dedication of her first printed book, in 1687, told Louis XIV how her training began. “Finding in me at the age of five some disposition for the harpsichord,” she wrote, “you ordered that care be taken to bring me up in it.” Cessac writes that she made her debut at court at that age, playing and singing before the king, and that he protected her and gave her the means to publish. Évrard Titon du Tillet, who gave her a long entry in his Parnasse françois of 1732, wrote that she was barely fifteen when she appeared at court, that the king took great pleasure in hearing her, and that Madame de Montespan kept her three or four years at her side to entertain herself and her visitors.
